rh-l2q2.summary: Holcot asks whether God knew from eternity that he would produce the world, and answers yes. The question becomes a broad treatment of eternity, truth, and future contingents. He denies that creatures had any eternal being, real or 'in God', other than being known. He treats talk of non-existents as properly false and counterfactually expounded. He denies that truth is an accident or the signified thing and identifies God as truth. He makes spoken propositions true only by convention. The eternity of the world is a neutral problem, though free creation from eternity is contradictory. God can always make a better world and do whatever does not make contradictories true together; impeccability comes by grace, against Ockham. Future contingents are determinately true, yet a true one could never have been true. God knows and can reveal them while they remain contingent, so scripture's predictions could be false and one can merit by false faith. God can assert falsehood and deceive the deserving but cannot lie. Rules of obligational disputation and the distinction between necessity of the consequence and of the consequent handle the paradoxes of prophecy and Christ's assertions.
claims: God knew from eternity that he would produce the world.
Future contingents are determinately true yet could never have been true.
Revealed futures remain contingent.
God can deceive but cannot lie.
Free creation from eternity is contradictory, though the world's eternity is undemonstrable.

rh-l2q2-Dd1e103.summary: Opening statement of the question: whether God knew from eternity that he would produce the world.

rh-l2q2-d1e105.summary: States the question: whether God knew from eternity that he would produce the world.

rh-l2q2-Dd1e120.summary: Ten principal arguments probe God's eternal knowledge of creation. Eternal truths would be other than God or identical with God. The divine essence would represent falsehoods or contradictories. Eternal election would imply eternal existence of the elect. Foreknowledge would exclude an eternal world, though such a world seems possible (Plato, Augustine's footprint, coeternal causes). Possible plural worlds raise questions of infinity, envy, the best, and the void. Future-tensed truth would imply necessity (Aristotle's sea battle). God's eternal present excludes foreknowledge (Boethius, Anselm). Creatures in God are God. Knowledge of future contingents would make the past necessary. Revelation of future contingents would either make scripture, prophecy, and Christ's words fallible or make them necessary, generating many casus about damnation, prophecy, angels, and prayer. Divine knowledge would be either necessary or mutable. Futures would be necessary at their first instant.
claims: Eternal knowledge of creation seems to conflict with contingency, eternity of the world, and the fallibility of revelation.

rh-l2q2-d1e125.summary: First principal argument: nothing other than God existed from eternity, and God's being about to produce the world is other than God, so it was not true from eternity and not known from eternity, since what is known is true when known.
claims: What is other than God was not true from eternity, so not known from eternity.

rh-l2q2-d1e149.summary: A reply: deny the minor. 'God will produce the world' was true from eternity, its truth existed from eternity, and only God existed from eternity, so that truth, i.e. God's being about to produce the world, was God.
claims: The eternal truth of a future-tensed proposition is God.

rh-l2q2-d1e171.summary: Confirmation from Anselm (Monologion 18; De veritate 1): it was always true that something would be, and never began to be true; truth has no beginning or end, else before it began it was true that there was no truth. Since probably for Anselm only God was eternal, that something was future was God.
claims: According to Anselm, truth has no beginning or end.
Eternal truth is God.

rh-l2q2-d1e217.summary: Against this: let a be the truth of 'God will produce the world'; a was God and a is not now God, so something was God that now is not.
claims: Identifying a contingent truth with God makes something cease to be God.

rh-l2q2-d1e227.summary: Further: a was God and a was the proposition, since a proposition's truth is not distinct from it (not an accident, which would make true sentences change, nor the thing signified, which per Anselm is the cause of truth), so the proposition was God.
claims: Truth of a proposition is the proposition itself.
If its truth were God, the proposition would be God.

rh-l2q2-d1e262.summary: Further: if God knew before creation that he would produce the world, the divine essence represented it so, and since it represents naturally, it still represents that God will produce the world, which is now false.
claims: The divine essence, representing naturally, would now represent a falsehood.

rh-l2q2-d1e280.summary: Fourth: the essence represents every truth, including 'God will not produce the world', and naturally and always, so before creation it represented both contradictories.
claims: The divine essence would represent contradictories.

rh-l2q2-d1e298.summary: Further: in the imagined measure before creation, if 'God wills to create the world' was true, he willed to create something other than himself, so something other than God was willed then, which could only be the world, so the world existed.
claims: Willing to create something other than God implies its existence.

rh-l2q2-d1e318.summary: Further: the saints were elected from eternity (Ephesians 1), so loved from eternity, so good from eternity, since God loves only the good, so men existed from eternity.
claims: Eternal election implies the eternal existence of the elect.

rh-l2q2-d1e331.summary: Further: if a names someone elect at the world's end, either God loves a, so a is something loved and so exists, or not, so a is not elect. And the divine essence represents the Antichrist's coming as naturally as a mental proposition does, so it will always represent it.
claims: Being loved by God implies being something.
The divine essence's natural representation of futures would be immutable.

rh-l2q2-d1e373.summary: Second principal argument: if God knew from eternity he would produce the world, he knew he had not yet produced it, so from that knowledge it follows formally that the world was not eternal, so he could not have produced the world from eternity.
claims: Foreknowledge of creation formally excludes an eternal world.

rh-l2q2-d1e401.summary: Further: if he could have produced it from eternity, posit it; then it was never to be produced, so he never knew he would produce it.
claims: An eternal world would never be 'to be produced'.

rh-l2q2-d1e412.summary: One reply: ignore the inference and grant that God could not have produced the world from eternity.
claims: God could not have produced the world from eternity.

rh-l2q2-d1e421.summary: Against: God can do no less by producing freely than if he produced naturally, and acting naturally he would have produced the world from eternity.
claims: A free agent can do whatever a natural one could.

rh-l2q2-d1e432.summary: Further: an eternal world involves no contradiction, so God could make it. Aristotle (Topics I) lists the world's eternity among undecidable problems; Plato held the world eternal yet having a beginning of constitution, like a footprint eternally under an eternal foot (Augustine); Augustine against Arius says the Son is coeternal as splendor with fire. So something can have an efficient cause and be coeternal with it.
claims: An eternal created world involves no contradiction.
A caused effect can be coeternal with its cause.

rh-l2q2-d1e478.summary: Further: before producing, he could have produced earlier, either only finitely earlier or infinitely. Not finitely, since for any earlier instant the same reason holds, so infinitely, so from eternity.
claims: If God could have created earlier at every time, he could have created from eternity.

rh-l2q2-d1e508.summary: Further: God was exactly the same before the instant of creation as at it, so whatever he willed at it he willed before, so the world existed before.
claims: God's immutability implies creation could not begin at an instant.

rh-l2q2-d1e521.summary: Further: if an eternal world were contradictory, temporal creation could be proved, and so an article of faith. And a rational will can have a free effect coeternal with it, as Christ's soul, had it been a wayfarer from eternity, would have had a meritorious act from eternity.
claims: If an eternal world were impossible, temporal creation would be demonstrable.

rh-l2q2-d1e545.summary: Confirmation: Dionysius says divine love did not permit God to be without offspring, and that love was eternal. Augustine's eternal foot and footprint and Chrysostom's eternal shrub and its image show coeternal effects. What is a perfection in secondary causes, having an effect without waiting for time, belongs to God, so he could produce the world from eternity.
claims: Producing a coeternal effect is a perfection to be attributed to God.

rh-l2q2-d1e591.summary: Third principal argument: did God know from eternity that he would produce several worlds? If not, he could not, and cannot now, though his power is the same and nothing impedes him.
claims: Either God foreknew many worlds or could not make them.

rh-l2q2-d1e609.summary: If he knew he would produce several worlds, then several worlds were and are understood by God, so some understood things are several worlds.
claims: Understood worlds would be something.

rh-l2q2-d1e620.summary: Further: he understands finitely or infinitely many possible worlds. Not finitely, since there is no stopping point; if infinitely, one infinite composite of them could revolve with diurnal motion, so an infinite body would move in finite time, against Aristotle.
claims: Infinitely many possible worlds imply an infinite body in finite motion.

rh-l2q2-d1e645.summary: Further: if God could have produced more worlds and did not, he was envious, by Augustine's reasoning that being able and unwilling to make good things would be great envy.
claims: Not making more worlds would be envy.

rh-l2q2-d1e670.summary: Confirmation: one who omits what is better does not do the best he can; two worlds are better than one, so God does not dispose all things best.
claims: Two worlds are better than one, so God did not do his best.

rh-l2q2-d1e688.summary: Confirmation from Augustine: whatever true reason shows better, know that God made it; so God has in fact made several worlds.
claims: According to Augustine, God made whatever reason shows better.

rh-l2q2-d1e699.summary: Further: if God knew he could produce another world a, why this rather than a? Without reason his will is irrational; with reason, since all are equal, he should have made none or infinitely many.
claims: Choosing among equal worlds requires reason, else irrational.

rh-l2q2-d1e719.summary: Further: could he have made a better world? If so, he did not do his best. If not, yet the world is finitely perfect so a better is possible; Lombard (I d. 44) and Augustine say God could have made man better, unable to sin, and so angel and universe.
claims: God could have made a better world, so did not do his best.

rh-l2q2-d1e750.summary: Further: if God could make another world located outside this one, what is there now? If something, something is beyond the world; if nothing, then where body can be and none is there is a vacuum, so a vacuum now exists.
claims: Possible extramundane worlds imply an actual vacuum.

rh-l2q2-d1e775.summary: Fourth principal argument: if 'God will produce the world' was true from eternity, one created before the world and asserting it would have spoken truly, so God produced the world necessarily.
claims: Antecedent truth of a future proposition implies necessity.

rh-l2q2-d1e793.summary: Confirmation from Aristotle (Peri hermeneias I): in contradictory future contingents neither part is determinately true, argued by reductio and ostensively.
claims: According to Aristotle, neither side of a future contingent contradiction is determinately true.

rh-l2q2-d1e813.summary: The reductio: if 'a will be' is true, one saying so speaks truly, so it must be as he says and cannot happen otherwise, so a happens necessarily, which Aristotle treats as impossible.
claims: If future contingents were true, they would happen necessarily.

rh-l2q2-d1e831.summary: The ostensive argument: as things are to being and not being, so propositions about them to truth and falsity; future things are indifferent, so their contradictories are neither true nor false. So if 'God will produce the world' were true from eternity, it would be true that God necessarily would, though he produced freely.
claims: Truth tracks the determination of things, so future contingents lack truth value.

rh-l2q2-d1e864.summary: Fifth principal argument: then God would have foreknowledge of the future, but Anselm says God's knowledge is not properly foreknowledge, since all is present to him, so the world was present to God from eternity.
claims: According to Anselm, God's knowledge is of the present, not foreknowledge.

rh-l2q2-d1e895.summary: Confirmation from Boethius: God sees all as if now occurring in his simple cognition; it is knowledge of a never-failing present, providence rather than prevision. Anselm (De concordia) says eternity contains all times as present time contains all places, and my action tomorrow is always present in eternity. So the world was present to God from eternity.
claims: According to Boethius and Anselm, all times are present to God's eternity.

rh-l2q2-d1e954.summary: Sixth principal argument: God would have known from eternity that he would create himself, since creatures are God: Augustine says what you seek in many is one in him; John 1 'what was made in him was life'; Anselm says whatever was made is life in him; and creating in God is the creative essence.
claims: Creatures in God are God, so creating them would be creating himself.

rh-l2q2-d1e983.summary: Seventh principal argument: did God produce the world necessarily or contingently? If necessarily, from eternity, since a natural sufficient cause yields its effect at once. If contingently, 'God will produce the world' was contingent before creation, and if known, true and contingent. So God would know one side of every future contingent contradiction, e.g. that Socrates will freely sin tomorrow (a). Either he began to know a, which is against Lombard, or knew it from eternity.
claims: Contingent creation implies God knows future contingents.
God cannot begin to know something.

rh-l2q2-d1e1029.summary: If from eternity: suppose 'a will be' was written on a wall yesterday; then 'what was written was true' is a true proposition about the past and so necessary, so Socrates necessarily sins.
claims: Past truth of a future contingent would necessitate it.

rh-l2q2-d1e1042.summary: Reply: 'a will be' is true but contingently, so though true it can never have been true; likewise 'God knew a would be' and 'what was written yesterday was true'. Propositions about the present or past equivalent to or depending on future ones differ from purely present or past ones: if 'Socrates sits' was true, 'it was true that Socrates sits' is necessary, but 'a was known by God' is true so that it could never have been true. Likewise 'Socrates was predestined'. If 'Socrates is predestined' is true, it was true from eternity and its opposite false, and neither can become true after the other.
claims: A true future contingent can be such that it never was true.
Past-tensed propositions that depend on the future are not necessary.
Truths about predestination are eternal yet contingent.

rh-l2q2-d1e1131.summary: Objection: if God knows contingent a will be, 'a will be' and 'a can fail to happen' stand together. Posit 'a will not happen'; then 'a will happen' was never true, though it was granted with no obligation, so you granted a falsehood.
claims: Positing the possible failure of a known future makes an earlier concession false.

rh-l2q2-d1e1149.summary: Further: yesterday you granted 'a will be' with no obligation; today asked 'a can fail', denying makes a necessary, granting and positing makes yesterday's concession false, so you responded badly yesterday.
claims: Contingency of the future makes past concessions retroactively false.

rh-l2q2-d1e1176.summary: Further: two propositions about before instant b can be true together or successively. 'a will be' and 'a will not be' are each contingent but cannot be true together, so successively, one true after the other before a occurs.
claims: Contradictory future contingents could be true successively.

rh-l2q2-d1e1204.summary: Further: if contradictories a and b are about the future, a true now and b possibly true tomorrow, then b can be true after a was true.
claims: A future contradictory can become true after the other was true.

rh-l2q2-d1e1217.summary: Further: whatever is not true now and can be true later can be true after being false; b is such.
claims: What is not true now but can be later can become true after falsity.

rh-l2q2-d1e1230.summary: Further: what is not future and can be future can begin to be future at some instant b; then immediately before b 'a was not future' was true, and so 'a will never be future'.
claims: Beginning to be future yields contradictions about prior truth.

rh-l2q2-d1e1254.summary: Further: if every proposition whose truth requires a future truth is contingent, then 'the sun is', 'the sun moves', 'God is first cause', 'Socrates runs', even 'I am' would be contingent and doubtful, since 'Socrates is' implies 'Socrates will be' (no last instant of a permanent thing), which God can falsify.
claims: Present truths implying future truths would all be contingent.

rh-l2q2-d1e1280.summary: Eighth principal argument: then God could reveal any future contingent, and it would remain contingent after revelation. Then scripture could be false (resurrection, judgment day), and by Augustine if one part could be false all could; one could merit in false faith; Abraham's true faith could become false; the blessed and angels could be deceived; I could make Christ's soul believe a falsehood or make Christ have asserted a falsehood or spoken against conscience.
claims: If revealed futures remain contingent, scripture, prophecy, and Christ's assertions could be false.

rh-l2q2-d1e1362.summary: Further: one justly damned a thousand years ago could have been unjustly damned. A Sadducee damned solely for believing 'there will be no resurrection' could never have believed a falsehood if the resurrection fails to occur.
claims: Contingent revealed truths make past damnations possibly unjust.

rh-l2q2-d1e1393.summary: Further: God reveals to Socrates that Plato will be saved and commands him to will it; Socrates envies Plato and is damned. A hundred years later with Plato alive, 'Plato will be damned' is still contingent; if so, Plato was never predestined, God never willed it, Socrates did not will against God and did not sin, so Plato can make Socrates unjustly damned.
claims: A future agent could retroactively make a past damnation unjust.

rh-l2q2-d1e1428.summary: Further: it would be in my power to make someone who lived a thousand years ago a prophet or not, since his prophecy about my doing a depends on my choice, and a false prophecy is no prophecy by definition.
claims: My choices would determine whether past persons were prophets.

rh-l2q2-d1e1452.summary: Further: Paul argues 'if the dead do not rise, neither did Christ' (1 Corinthians 15), and Augustine says the Apostle's connections hold. The consequent is impossible, so the antecedent; if it were contingent the inference would fail, or God could make Christ never have risen. Likewise Micaiah's 'if you return in peace, the Lord has not spoken by me' (1 Kings 22).
claims: Scriptural conditionals treat revealed futures as necessary.

rh-l2q2-d1e1490.summary: Further: 'Christ's soul is blessed' would be contingent, since it was certain of eternal beatitude, yet it can be annihilated, so could never have been certain, so never blessed.
claims: Possible annihilation would undermine the certainty and beatitude of Christ's soul.

rh-l2q2-d1e1514.summary: Further: God could not make anyone certain of the future, nor could anyone believe his promises without deception, since after any assertion he could do otherwise. But 'God is faithful, he cannot deny himself' (2 Timothy 2), and Christ said all written of him must be fulfilled (Luke 24), so necessarily.
claims: Contingent promises would make divine certainty impossible.

rh-l2q2-d1e1558.summary: Further: then angels would not be confirmed nor the devil adjudged to eternal punishment; angels could sin and the devil merit; Christ and all preachers could have spoken falsely and the whole faith be false, and God have deceived those he taught.
claims: Contingency of revealed futures would unsettle confirmation, damnation, and the faith.

rh-l2q2-d1e1594.summary: Further: revelation causes no less certainty than prophecy, which by definition announces events with immobile truth, so whatever is prophesied is immobilely and necessarily future.
claims: Prophecy announces events with immobile truth.

rh-l2q2-d1e1618.summary: Further: what is so future that it cannot become non-future before it is present happens necessarily, and whatever God proposes to do is such (Anselm: God's will makes truth immutable). Anselm also says the Virgin's faith that her son would die was true and it was necessary it so happen. So 'this will be is contingent' and 'this will be is revealed by God' are incompossible.
claims: According to Anselm, what God proposes to do is immutably future.
Revealed futures are necessary.

rh-l2q2-d1e1662.summary: Further: if one must believe a prophecy could fail, one need not believe the prophet or God, and the Jews were not bound to believe the prophets about the Messiah, since the opposite could happen.
claims: Contingent prophecy would remove the obligation to believe.

rh-l2q2-d1e1688.summary: Further, that God cannot reveal future contingents: if he reveals to Socrates in charity that he will sin mortally tomorrow, Socrates may lawfully will it, conforming to God's will, yet willing to be in mortal sin is mortal sin. Also contradictories would hold: he will sin and, knowing he would be miserable, cannot will to sin (Anselm).
claims: Revealing someone's future sin would make willing it both licit and sinful.

rh-l2q2-d1e1733.summary: Further: if God revealed to Socrates that he will be damned, Socrates must believe and so despair, and God would be author of his despair and so of sin.
claims: Revealing damnation would make God author of despair.

rh-l2q2-d1e1749.summary: Further: God reveals to Gabriel that Socrates will always be in charity and commands him to help Socrates while in charity. Socrates remains free and sins; then Gabriel both must and need not help him.
claims: A revealed perseverance plus Socrates' freedom yields contradictory obligations.

rh-l2q2-d1e1776.summary: Further: if God reveals to Socrates in charity that he will be damned, can he justly pray for his salvation? If so, he wills against God's revealed will, and the Church could pray for those it knows damned, against Augustine (City of God XXI), who says it would not pray for them any more than for the devil. So revealed truths are not contingent after revelation.
claims: According to Augustine, the Church would not pray for those known to be damned.

rh-l2q2-d1e1824.summary: If he cannot justly pray: as a wayfarer he must will his salvation, being in charity he loves himself for beatitude, he cannot not will beatitude, and he must love himself as he loves his neighbor, so he may pray for himself.
claims: A wayfarer in charity must will and may pray for his salvation.

rh-l2q2-d1e1859.summary: Further: 'Peter will deny Christ' would be contingent after Christ's assertion 'you will deny me three times', so Christ could have asserted a falsehood.
claims: Christ's prediction of Peter's denial would be contingent.

rh-l2q2-d1e1875.summary: Further: 'Christ sweated for fear of future death' would be contingent and could be false, so he would have sweated without cause and been deceived.
claims: Christ's agony would be groundless if his death were contingent.

rh-l2q2-d1e1886.summary: Further: 'Gabriel saw in the Word that judgment day will be' would be contingent, yet Gabriel revealed it to Daniel, which is now necessary, and he revealed only what he saw in the Word.
claims: Angelic vision in the Word would be contingent though its revelation is past.

rh-l2q2-d1e1910.summary: Further: if what is ordained remains contingent, it is in Socrates' power to make God have predestined or reprobated him from eternity, so he could cause his own eternal predestination and God's election would depend on the created will.
claims: Human choice would cause eternal predestination.

rh-l2q2-d1e1935.summary: Further: an angel, perfect in natural knowledge but unconfirmed, sees in the Word that Socrates will commit homicide and be punished, is commanded to will only what it sees God will, wills Socrates' punishment, and is confirmed for that act. If Socrates may not sin, the angel was confirmed without merit or even for mortal sin, having willed what God never willed. Similarly a man in charity commanded to will only what seems reasonable, shown a future a against his own reasoning, wills a; if a fails, he willed without reason and sinned mortally while in charity.
claims: Contingent revealed futures could make confirmation rest on sin and charity coexist with mortal sin.

rh-l2q2-d1e2093.summary: Further: if what is revealed remains contingent, God could make the past not past, against Aristotle and Agathon (Ethics VI). Since God revealed to Peter that judgment day will be, its truth is past; God can make it not be, so the truth never was in Peter.
claims: Contingent revealed truths would let God undo the past.

rh-l2q2-d1e2141.summary: Ninth principal argument: God knew future contingents necessarily or contingently. If necessarily, he would have known 'Antichrist will be' even had he willed to create nothing. If contingently, it was possible he did not know them, and then he could create nothing, since nothing is produced unknowingly, so would not be omnipotent. And if he knows Antichrist necessarily, Antichrist cannot fail to be and God cannot will otherwise.
claims: Divine knowledge of future contingents is neither necessary nor contingent without absurdity.

rh-l2q2-d1e2185.summary: If God knows freely, he can cease to know it, and then cannot create or will Antichrist. And if knowledge of 'Antichrist will be' can cease, some change occurs in God or creature, not in the creature, so God could make a proposition true after it was not without any change. Tenth principal argument: whatever is future is necessarily future: at instant a, 'Antichrist necessarily will be' is true, since a permanent thing lasts beyond its first instant.
claims: Cessation of divine knowledge would imply change in God.
At its first instant, a future thing necessarily will continue.

rh-l2q2-d1e2265.summary: Further: if Antichrist will be contingently at a, then since at a he will necessarily be, he will be contingently when he necessarily will be.
claims: Contingent and necessary futurity would coincide.

rh-l2q2-d1e2285.summary: For the opposite: God produced the world voluntarily and freely, so before producing willed to produce it and knew nothing would impede his will, so knew the world would be produced by him; and he never began to know this, so knew it from eternity.
claims: God knew from eternity that he would produce the world.

rh-l2q2-Dd1e2302.summary: Holcot answers yes and announces ten inquiries on the eternal being of creatures, being in God, understanding non-existents, truth and propositions, the eternity of the world, a better world, future contingents, revelation, contingency of the revealed, and replies.
claims: God knew from eternity that he would produce the world.

rh-l2q2-d1e2307.summary: Holcot answers yes, and lists ten inquiries: whether creatures had being from eternity distinct from God; whether creatures have being in God; whether 'a rose is understood' is true when no rose exists; whether truth is distinct from the proposition; whether God could have produced the world from eternity; whether he could have made a better world; whether future propositions have determinate truth; whether God can cause knowledge of future contingents by revelation; whether what is revealed remains contingent; and replies.
claims: God knew from eternity that he would produce the world.

rh-l2q2-Dd1e2353.summary: Holcot denies that creatures had any eternal being distinct from God, whether quidditative, potential, or representative, since that would make them eternally real and never created.
claims: Creatures had no eternal being distinct from God.

rh-l2q2-d1e2358.summary: First article: things other than God had no being from eternity distinct from God, neither quidditative, potential, nor representative being, as some ancients held. Otherwise every thing would have been a real thing from eternity, Socrates would have been Socrates eternally and never created or begotten, the whole world would be eternal, and the Antichrist would now exist and nothing would be future.
claims: Creatures had no being of any kind from eternity distinct from God.

rh-l2q2-Dd1e2401.summary: Creatures are not properly in God, but only improperly, as known and producible by him, as Lombard and Augustine explain.
claims: Creatures are in God only as known and producible.

rh-l2q2-d1e2409.summary: Second article: whether creatures had any being in God from eternity.

rh-l2q2-d1e2416.summary: Properly nothing is in another except as located in place, part in whole, or form in subject, and creatures were in God in none of these ways. The saints say creatures are in God improperly, because he knows and can produce them, as a servant is 'in' his lord's power or a work in the artisan. Lombard (I d. 36): all things are said to be in God not because creature is creator but because they are always in his knowledge, which is life.
claims: Creatures are not properly in God.
Creatures are 'in God' only as known and producible by him.

rh-l2q2-d1e2453.summary: No greater difficulty: Lombard says Augustine explains such phrases (all things present to God, in God, with God, life in him) as meaning that ineffable knowledge of all things is in him.
claims: 'All things are in God' means God knows all things.

rh-l2q2-Dd1e2470.summary: On whether 'a rose is understood' is true when no rose exists, Holcot sets out an opinion granting it by ampliation, supported by memory, contrition, foresight, artistry, final causality, Augustine, and Aristotle. He then argues for the contrary: properly such propositions are false, as Augustine's account of time in Confessions XI confirms. They are granted improperly as abbreviations, for example 'there is an intellection that would be of the rose if it existed'. The dispute is largely verbal.
claims: Properly, 'a non-existent is understood' is false.
Such propositions are expounded counterfactually.

rh-l2q2-d1e2478.summary: Third article: when no rose exists, are 'a rose is conceived/understood' true? One view says yes: such verbs can be verified of terms suppositing for nothing as for things; what is nothing is intelligible, and we form propositions and concepts about non-beings, the predicate inhering 'as if it were'. Anselm (De casu diaboli 11) is cited: many things are said 'according to the form of speaking' that are nothing in reality, like blindness, and evil signifies something only in that way.
claims: According to some, 'the rose is understood' is true though no rose exists.
According to Anselm, many expressions signify something only by form of speech.

rh-l2q2-d1e2562.summary: Arguments for it: everyone experiences that he can think of and remember a dead man, else one could not grieve a father's death or pray for his soul.
claims: We can remember the dead.

rh-l2q2-d1e2573.summary: Further: otherwise we could not be contrite for or confess past sins, nor provide for the future, being unable to think of it.
claims: Contrition and foresight require thinking of non-existents.

rh-l2q2-d1e2583.summary: Further: man naturally fears death, so thinks of death; hope and desire are only of future things, so future things are hoped for and understood.
claims: Fear, hope, and desire concern non-existents.

rh-l2q2-d1e2592.summary: Further: every free agent premeditates its work, as a builder imagines the house and a painter the statue.
claims: Artisans conceive their works before they exist.

rh-l2q2-d1e2599.summary: Further: whoever acts for an end understands the end before it exists; it is not in the soul, since then it would be a moved agent (Metaphysics XII), but is pre-understood as existing outside the soul, where it is not yet.
claims: The end is understood before it exists.

rh-l2q2-d1e2617.summary: Further: Augustine (City of God XI) says God made nothing unknowingly; the world could not be known to us unless it existed, but could not exist unless known to God.
claims: According to Augustine, God knew the world before it existed.

rh-l2q2-d1e2635.summary: Further: Augustine (De trinitate XV): God knows creatures not because they are, but they are because he knows them; he knew them as to be created as he knows them created.
claims: According to Augustine, creatures exist because God knows them.

rh-l2q2-d1e2648.summary: Further: if you saw Socrates kill Plato and then God annihilated both, you could still remember and testify; to deny this is to deny sense.
claims: One can remember and testify about annihilated things.

rh-l2q2-d1e2660.summary: Further: we believe many things of Christ, his birth, death, resurrection, judgment day, the Antichrist; believing the Jews killed Christ, you conceive Jews and death.
claims: Belief about past and future events requires conceiving them.

rh-l2q2-d1e2680.summary: Further: if only beings could be understood, two conclusions against Aristotle would follow: 'Caesar is in opinion, so Caesar exists' would be valid, though Aristotle denies 'Homer is a poet, so Homer is'; and the second reading of 'b may be a' (what may be b may be a) would be unintelligible.
claims: Restricting understanding to beings contradicts Aristotle's logic.

rh-l2q2-d1e2711.summary: Further: Aristotle discussed the infinite and the void, so understood what cannot be. The contrary opinion: if Socrates' intellection of a rose is conserved after the rose is destroyed, 'something is understood by Socrates' and 'a rose is understood' are to be denied, and likewise now 'Antichrist is understood by God', and before creation 'God understands the world'.
claims: On the contrary view, 'a rose is understood' is false when no rose exists.

rh-l2q2-d1e2740.summary: Argument for it: a universal is true if each singular is; in the case, each singular of 'nothing is understood by Socrates' is true, and the particular 'something is understood by Socrates' has no true singular.
claims: Inductively, nothing is understood when the object does not exist.

rh-l2q2-d1e2760.summary: Further: in 'a rose is understood by Socrates', the subject supposits for something, so a rose is something, or for nothing, so nothing is understood.
claims: The subject term must supposit for something or nothing.

rh-l2q2-d1e2771.summary: Further: everything that is something is God or a creature, and what Socrates understands would be something.
claims: Whatever is something is God or creature.

rh-l2q2-d1e2779.summary: Further: if your father is dead and you have only an intellection of him, either something is understood, so your father is something, or nothing, so you understand and understand nothing.
claims: Thinking of the dead either makes them something or is understanding nothing.

rh-l2q2-d1e2795.summary: Further: what God understands is something understood by God; Antichrist is understood by God, so is something.
claims: Being understood implies being something.

rh-l2q2-d1e2804.summary: Further: the first view would grant 'a chimera is a chimera' and 'Antichrist is Antichrist', since something understood is Antichrist, and a present-tense subject without ampliation converts with 'something that is Antichrist is Antichrist'.
claims: The first view implies 'a chimera is a chimera' is true.

rh-l2q2-d1e2834.summary: Further: an affirmative present-tense proposition requires the predicate's referent to be the subject's. By parity, if God conserved vision or touch with the object destroyed, Socrates would touch his annihilated father, which is absurd.
claims: By parity, conserved sensation would imply touching what does not exist.

rh-l2q2-d1e2856.summary: Further: Augustine (Confessions XI): when past things are truly narrated, not the things themselves but words conceived from their images are drawn from memory; we see not future things but present signs. There are not three times but the present of past (memory), of present (attention), and of future (expectation). Few things are spoken properly. So properly only what exists is known; 'Caesar is known' is said because a species that would be his, if he existed, is known.
claims: According to Augustine, only present images and signs are properly known.
Past and future are known through present memory and expectation.

rh-l2q2-d1e2954.summary: Further: if these verbs ampliated, 'what is not known is known by you' would be true. The dispute is more verbal than real. Such propositions must be distinguished: taken properly, by the force of the words, they are false, since 'Antichrist is understood' converts with 'Antichrist is understood' in the present without ampliation. Taken improperly, at the users' will, they stand for true ones: 'there is an intellection that would be of Antichrist if he existed'. So properly 'a rose is understood' with no rose, 'Antichrist is understood by God', 'my father's soul is understood by me' are to be denied, though granted improperly.
claims: The dispute about understanding non-existents is mostly verbal.
Properly, 'a non-existent is understood' is false.
Improperly it stands for 'there is an intellection that would be of it if it existed'.

rh-l2q2-d1e3038.summary: Reply to the Anselm argument: Anselm himself says 'this' and 'something' are said only of what is, and that speaking of non-beings is not proper speech about things; 'blindness is in the eye' taken properly is false.
claims: Anselm supports treating talk of non-beings as improper.

rh-l2q2-d1e3058.summary: Reply to remembering the dead: 'I remember a dead man' is false, with an opposition in the predicate. 'I remember Caesar' is granted vulgarly for 'I have knowledge that Caesar was', and Caesar was and is not; as Augustine says, what I know is Caesar's image, caused when he existed. It abbreviates three propositions: there is in me a cognition that would be of Caesar if he existed, Caesar was known by me, and Caesar is not.
claims: 'I remember Caesar' abbreviates a conjunction of three propositions.

rh-l2q2-d1e3107.summary: Reply on contrition: one is contrite for sins in having a cognition by which sins would be thought of if they existed, which causes sorrow; literally the proposition is false and must be expounded otherwise than the words suggest.
claims: Contrition for past sins is expounded through present cognitions.

rh-l2q2-d1e3127.summary: Reply on foresight: future things are not properly foreseen, since nothing is future, distinguishing future from present (Anselm). We use many terms as if they stood for things when they do not, speaking falsely if properly taken, as 'he is thinking of buying cloth'. The difficulty lies in expounding talk about the future: 'a man will be Antichrist', read as 'what will be a man is Antichrist', is contradictory, since 'what' always exercises its signification for a being.
claims: Future things are not properly foreseen.
Talk about the future must be expounded to avoid contradiction.

rh-l2q2-Dd1e3174.summary: Holcot argues that truth and falsity are not inherent accidents of propositions, which would let flies change angels' minds, nor the signified things, which would make contradictories share truth. God, however, is a truth distinct from every proposition. In a nested doubt he asks whether spoken propositions can be true, given that they are successive, natural and conventional in signification, indexical, language-relative, and possibly unheard. He concludes that spoken sentences are literally neither true nor false. By human convention they are judged as if existing whole at their last instant. They have no natural propositional signification, signification is aptitudinal, and one can alter what a sentence signifies to oneself.
claims: Truth is neither an accident of propositions nor the signified thing.
God is truth distinct from propositions.
Spoken sentences are judged true or false by convention.

rh-l2q2-d1e3182.summary: Fourth article: whether truth and falsity are distinct from the propositions called true and false.

rh-l2q2-d1e3189.summary: Three things. First, truth and falsity are not absolute accidents inhering in propositions, distinct from them. Proved four ways.
claims: Truth and falsity are not inherent accidents of propositions.

rh-l2q2-d1e3200.summary: First: otherwise moving my finger would change an angel's mind, and a fly flying would change all angels and books where 'no animal moves' is written; the fly would act at infinite distance, I could alter Christ's soul, and the devil would continually alter good angels.
claims: If truth were an accident, distant events would change minds and books.

rh-l2q2-d1e3238.summary: Further: then substance would not be the only thing receptive of contraries without change in itself, against the Categories, which says a proposition becomes true or false without changing, because the thing is or is not.
claims: According to the Categories, propositions change truth value without intrinsic change.

rh-l2q2-d1e3251.summary: Further: 'God creates something new' can be false, so its falsity can exist; if God cannot create it, something can exist that God cannot create; if he can, creating it makes something created anew, so the proposition would be true and false.
claims: Truth as an entity leads to contradictions about God's creating it.

rh-l2q2-d1e3280.summary: Fourth: 'God creates nothing' can be true; if its truth can be created, then creating it makes 'something is created' true together with 'nothing is created'.
claims: Creating the truth of 'God creates nothing' would be contradictory.

rh-l2q2-d1e3302.summary: Second: a proposition's truth is not the thing signified, since then propositions with non-referring terms would have no truth, like 'Caesar is not a chimera', 'every animal was in Noah's ark', 'a man will be Antichrist', 'white can be black'.
claims: Truth is not the signified thing, since some true propositions signify no existing thing.

rh-l2q2-d1e3320.summary: Further: contradictories signify the same things, so would have the same truth and be true and false together.
claims: Contradictories signify the same things, so truth cannot be the thing signified.

rh-l2q2-d1e3331.summary: Further: 'man runs' and 'man does not run' would be convertible, and God and the devil would be one falsity, that of 'God is the devil'.
claims: Identifying truth with signified things yields absurd identities.

rh-l2q2-d1e3343.summary: Third: there is a truth really distinct from any proposition, so 'truth' is not said univocally of it and of propositions. If truth is a thing signifying wholly as things are, that thing is God (Augustine; Anselm, De veritate), the truth of every true proposition, since the divine essence signifies to whomever it wills, and to itself naturally, as things are, being a cognition always conforming to every true proposition. An angel's knowledge is an incomplex truth equivalent to our complex knowledge, if angels do not compose and divide. Now to propositions used among humans to communicate concepts.
claims: God is a truth distinct from every proposition.
'Truth' is equivocal between God and propositions.
The divine essence is a cognition conforming to every true proposition.
Angelic knowledge is incomplex but equivalent to complex knowledge.

rh-l2q2-Dd1e3394.summary: Doubts about whether spoken propositions can be true or false. Holcot raises their successive existence, partial utterance, natural signification of sounds, anaphora, indexicals like 'I am Robert', diversity of languages, and unheard speech. He answers that spoken sentences are literally neither true nor false, being successive collections of sound-qualities, but are by convention judged as if whole at their last instant. They signify only by imposition, cause one mental proposition, and signify aptitudinally. Respondents answer according to the mental proposition caused in them, and reading requires imagination of the corresponding sounds.
claims: Spoken sentences are true or false only by convention.
Signification is conventional and aptitudinal.
Respondents judge by the mental proposition caused in them.

rh-l2q2-d1e3402.summary: Doubts about such propositions. First: whether a spoken proposition can be true or false.

rh-l2q2-d1e3409.summary: It seems not: what does not exist is neither true nor false, and a spoken proposition never exists whole, since when the subject is, the predicate is not, as speech is successive.
claims: A spoken proposition never exists whole.

rh-l2q2-d1e3427.summary: Further: if Socrates utters 'no man is an ass', when does he utter truth? Not at any word, since no term is true, and when he utters the first he utters only 'no', which is not truth.
claims: No moment of utterance contains a true proposition.

rh-l2q2-d1e3463.summary: A reply: 'is uttered' can mean being in utterance or having been uttered. In the first sense, uttering a part is being in utterance of the whole, so true; in the second not. Against this: then when uttering 'no man is' he utters a falsehood before 'no man is an ass', so utters truth and falsehood at once, knowingly, speaking according to and against conscience.
claims: Being in utterance of a whole leads to uttering truth and falsehood at once.
concepts: in fieri and in facto esse

rh-l2q2-d1e3511.summary: Further: uttering 'God is, man is animal' one begins to utter falsehood by beginning to utter 'God is', which is absurd.
claims: Beginning an utterance would commit one to its partial content.

rh-l2q2-d1e3527.summary: Further: if Plato hears only 'God is' during hour a while Socrates utters a longer copulative, then whatever Socrates uttered in a was heard by Plato, only truth was heard, so Socrates uttered only truth and not the whole copulative.
claims: Partial hearing implies only part was uttered.

rh-l2q2-d1e3545.summary: Further: by the same reasoning, uttering the last syllable would be uttering the whole and so the middle.
claims: Uttering any part would be uttering every part.

rh-l2q2-d1e3558.summary: Further: one would have uttered truth and could never have, or lied and could never have, since after 'no man is' he may freely add 'an ass' or not.
claims: The truth of an utterance would depend on its future completion.

rh-l2q2-d1e3578.summary: Further: no spoken affirmative can be true, since 'man is animal' signifies by imposition that man is animal and naturally that the term 'man' is the term 'animal', which is false; signification by imposition does not remove natural signification.
claims: Spoken propositions naturally signify identity of their terms, which is false.

rh-l2q2-d1e3618.summary: Further: the terms generate two intentions in a hearer, of the sounds and of the things, the first more essential, and the first is false. Since a natural agent causes like effects in like patients, the uninstructed and instructed hearer receive the same intention of the sounds, so the utterance is false.
claims: Spoken words naturally cause a false proposition about the words themselves.

rh-l2q2-d1e3689.summary: Confirmation: causing intentions like the sounds belongs to the utterance naturally, causing intentions of the signified things only by convention, so it more essentially causes a false proposition.
claims: Natural signification is more essential than conventional.

rh-l2q2-d1e3722.summary: Further: in 'some man is Socrates and he is Plato', the second part is false (Socrates is Plato), yet the same words are part of the true 'some man disputes and he is Plato', so true and false.
claims: Anaphoric parts can be true and false depending on context.

rh-l2q2-d1e3740.summary: Further: written 'I am Robert' is false as read by others and true as read by Robert, so the same written proposition is true and false.
claims: Indexical written propositions are true or false depending on the reader.

rh-l2q2-d1e3769.summary: Further: a proposition is true because things are as it signifies by imposition, but languages differ; if in some language 'man is animal' means man is a stone, a speaker heard by both a Latin and a barbarian would speak truly and falsely, and any proposition could be doubtful.
claims: Conventional signification varies by language, making truth relative.

rh-l2q2-d1e3811.summary: Confirmation: no single person imposed all languages, and any community is free to use a term as it wishes, so the Latin and barbarian rightly judge the same utterance true and false.
claims: Communities freely impose meanings, so one utterance can be true and false.

rh-l2q2-d1e3843.summary: Further: if a deaf Socrates utters 'God is' and no one hears, the utterance is neither false (it signifies nothing otherwise than things are) nor true (its terms signify to no one).
claims: An unheard utterance signifies nothing and so is neither true nor false.

rh-l2q2-d1e3865.summary: Confirmation from Augustine's definition of a sign as what brings something else to cognition through the senses; an unheard utterance does neither, so is no sign. Further: then I could make the Gospel contain nothing true by closing the book, since unread writing signifies nothing.
claims: According to Augustine's definition, an unperceived sign is no sign.

rh-l2q2-d1e3908.summary: Further: Socrates can make any proposition signify to him otherwise than things are, so make it signify falsely to him, and so make the whole Bible false.
claims: Individual reinterpretation would make scripture false.

rh-l2q2-d1e3926.summary: For this doubt one must see what a spoken proposition has by nature and what by institution.

rh-l2q2-d1e3933.summary: By nature it has four: it is produced successively; its parts do not remain; it is a multitude of sounds, which Aristotle classes as discrete quantity, so 'spoken sentence' is a collective name for many things not making one per se; since a sound is a quality generated by striking bodies and the medium, a sentence is many qualities. And it is a natural sign of the speaker's imagination.
claims: A spoken sentence is a collection of successive sound-qualities.
Speech naturally signifies the speaker's imagination.

rh-l2q2-d1e3966.summary: By imposition it signifies whatever external thing people will, and languages differ by different impositions. So every true proposition could become false and conversely if all changed the meanings. Its significant terms are taken significatively by human institution, except in certain propositions, so they must be distinguished.
claims: Conventional signification depends on imposition and can change.

rh-l2q2-d1e3993.summary: A true proposition signifies as things are and not otherwise; a false one the reverse. The same proposition can be true and false, but no true proposition is a false proposition. 'God is man is animal' is false and impossible as signifying that 'God is' is 'man is animal', and true and necessary as being its two true parts. In a copulative this seems clear, though one may say the copulative includes the copula and so is not just the two propositions.
claims: The same string can be a true and a false proposition, but no true proposition is a false one.

rh-l2q2-d1e4065.summary: By human institution a spoken proposition is answered as if it existed whole at the instant its utterance ends, though in fact it never does, being successive. 'This sentence is true: God is' means it would be true if it existed whole and signified only that God exists. A respondent may doubt whether any proposition is true, since in another language it may signify otherwise, so 'true to me, so true' fails, though 'false to me, so false' holds. A respondent does well to grant what is true to him in the shared language; so one may rightly grant a falsehood or deny a truth, as 'you are not speaking' put to a silent person.
claims: By convention a spoken proposition is judged as if whole at its last instant.
'True to me' does not imply 'true'.
A good respondent may grant a falsehood or deny a truth.

rh-l2q2-d1e4128.summary: If one says 'man is not animal' and another reverses it 'animal is not man', these are two specifically distinct propositions though no word differs in species, since the order of terms constitutes the proposition.
claims: Word order makes specifically distinct propositions from the same words.

rh-l2q2-d1e4164.summary: Reply to the first argument: no spoken sentence is true or false in reality, since it never exists. But because sentences are instruments of speech, it is instituted that they be judged as if they were permanent things existing whole at the last instant of utterance; 'this sentence God is is true' means that if it were permanent and signified God exists, it would be true. Grammar and logic should be learned once for all by use and institution.
claims: No spoken sentence is literally true or false.
Spoken sentences are judged by a convention treating them as permanent.

rh-l2q2-d1e4216.summary: Reply to the second: grants 'Socrates utters truth' in the sense of being in the course of uttering truth, and simultaneously falsehood, but judgment of what is uttered follows the whole intended utterance, by human institution. So one is called truthful or a liar by the whole sentence one intends, not a part. 'God is man is animal' is proper and intelligible, and from beginning to utter 'God is' it does not follow that one utters a falsehood.
claims: Truthfulness is judged by the whole intended utterance.

rh-l2q2-d1e4267.summary: Reply to the third: grants Socrates uttered only truth in a, though 'Socrates utters falsehood' was true in the sense of being in the course of uttering, so he utters truth and falsehood, whole and parts at once.
claims: One can be in the course of uttering both truth and falsehood.

rh-l2q2-d1e4280.summary: Reply to the fourth: grants that being in utterance of the last term is being in utterance of the whole, taking 'whole' categorematically.
claims: Uttering the last term is uttering the whole, categorematically.

rh-l2q2-d1e4296.summary: Reply to the fifth: denies the inference and consequent. If he uttered truth, necessarily he uttered truth. After the first syllable 'it was true that Socrates utters truth' (being in utterance) does not imply 'Socrates uttered truth'; with another reading of 'utters' the inference holds but the antecedent is false.
claims: Being in the course of uttering truth does not imply having uttered truth.

rh-l2q2-d1e4320.summary: Reply to the sixth: the spoken 'man is animal' signifies nothing naturally, but only by its conventional signification, and in no way denotes naturally that the term 'man' is the term 'animal'.
claims: Spoken propositions have no natural propositional signification.

rh-l2q2-d1e4336.summary: Reply to the seventh: each significant term may cause two intentions, one of the sound and one of the thing, but the proposition causes only one mental proposition. A magpie hearing 'man is animal' has in its imagination species of the sounds that represent only the sounds; three such intentions are a heap, not a proposition, since a proposition requires a term functioning as a copula, conventionally or naturally. So of six intentions caused in a hearer, the three of the sounds are no proposition and the three of the things are one.
claims: Intentions of sounds form a heap, not a proposition.
A proposition requires a functioning copula.
A spoken proposition causes only one mental proposition.

rh-l2q2-d1e4465.summary: Reply to the eighth: the second part of 'some man is Socrates and he is Plato' is false, and a verbally identical part of 'some man disputes and Plato is he' may be true. With proper names or demonstrative or relative pronouns, verbally identical propositions can differ in truth, since 'he' refers to Socrates in one and Plato in the other.
claims: Verbally identical propositions with pronouns can differ in truth.

rh-l2q2-d1e4495.summary: Reply to the ninth: the written 'I am Robert' is neither true nor false, since the written 'I' signifies only the spoken 'I', which signifies the speaker when uttered with imagination. A reader named Robert speaks truly, another falsely, both reading correctly, but the writing itself is neither. To read is not merely to utter the equivalent while seeing it; a magpie trained to say it while seeing the book does not read, nor a layman reciting the Lord's Prayer. Reading requires that the writing, by sight, cause an imagination of the corresponding sounds which one then utters.
claims: Written indexical propositions are neither true nor false.
Reading requires that seeing writing cause imagination of the corresponding sounds.

rh-l2q2-d1e4569.summary: Reply to the tenth: a whole proposition can be equivocal by chance or design, as a term can. 'God is' might signify to a barbarian that man is an ass, but it does not follow that a true proposition is a false proposition, only that such a string is a false proposition. A respondent should answer according to the mental proposition the utterance causes in him: the Latin rightly grants, the barbarian rightly denies, each assuming it signifies only what his mental proposition says.
claims: Whole propositions can be equivocal.
A respondent answers according to the mental proposition caused in him.

rh-l2q2-d1e4634.summary: Reply to the eleventh: if a deaf man utters 'God is', the complex signifies truly and he utters a true proposition, since it is instituted to signify and things are as it signifies; though it signifies to no one actually, it is apt to signify. 'It signifies to no one, so does not signify' fails, and terms in the definition of sign that sound actual should be read as aptitudinal.
claims: Signification is aptitudinal, not actual.
An unheard utterance can be true.

rh-l2q2-d1e4663.summary: Reply to the twelfth: if Socrates changes the meanings of terms, hearing 'God is' he may form 'a dog runs', and so a man can falsify the whole Bible and all the articles for himself. Objection: one man cannot change the meaning without others' consent. Denied: he can make it signify otherwise to himself, false for him though true for others, since 'true to him, so true' fails though 'false to him, so false' holds.
claims: One can change what a proposition signifies to oneself.
Private reinterpretation falsifies scripture only for oneself.

rh-l2q2-Dd1e4703.summary: Holcot holds that the world's eternity is a neutral problem, neither demonstrable nor refutable, but that 'the world was freely created from eternity' is contradictory, since free production from non-being implies prior non-being. He supports this with astronomical and genealogical arguments. Against the standard infinity arguments for a beginning, he denies there is an actual infinite quantity to traverse. Every magnitude contains infinitely many proportional parts, and distributive truths do not yield collective ones. One infinite can exceed another only across kinds (unlike Grosseteste's view). A part can equal its whole. The soul's immortality is known by faith alone.
claims: The eternity of the world is a neutral problem.
Free creation from eternity is contradictory.
Standard infinity arguments against an eternal world fail.
The immortality of the soul is known by faith alone.

rh-l2q2-d1e4711.summary: Fifth article, on whether God could have produced the world from eternity. Three theses: 'the world was from eternity' cannot be demonstrated or refuted, a neutral problem (Topics I); likewise 'the world was created, conserved, or produced by God from eternity'; but 'the world was created or effectively produced by God from eternity' involves a contradiction. Proof: whatever freely produces something from non-being to being first understood it not to be before being, and an eternally produced world was never understood by God not to be. Everything brought from non-being was first in potency and began to be.
claims: The eternity of the world is neither demonstrable nor refutable.
An eternal world freely created from non-being is contradictory.
What is produced from non-being began to be.

rh-l2q2-d1e4781.summary: Further: if the world was freely produced from eternity, God knew 'God creates the world' at some time, and with it 'and immediately before the world was not'. Whether creation was instantaneous at a or successive over finite time, the world begins; over infinite time it would never be produced. Against the reply denying that God knew the copulative: then he knew the world existed before, implying destruction and renewal, which is nothing.
claims: Creation, instantaneous or successive, implies a beginning.

rh-l2q2-d1e4879.summary: Further: if the sun was created from eternity, it was at some degree a of a zodiac sign. If it moved there, it was not created there; if not, after an hour at a it entered the next degree b, so it began moving and was not eternal.
claims: An eternal sun's motion would have a beginning.

rh-l2q2-d1e4915.summary: Further: if created at the head of Aries, God knew 'the sun is in Aries and never was before, and a year will pass before it returns', so the first year of the world began.
claims: Solar position at creation marks a first year.

rh-l2q2-d1e4943.summary: Further: at its creation the sun lit either our hemisphere or the antipodes', so one first day preceded the other and time is finite.
claims: The first illumination fixes a first day.

rh-l2q2-d1e4963.summary: Further: if the sun was created at instant a and then eclipsed, the interval to the first eclipse is finite, so the sun began.
claims: A first eclipse after finite time implies the sun began.

rh-l2q2-d1e4983.summary: Further: if God produced the world from eternity and knows 'God cannot make the world not to have been', either it was always true, so God never could, so did not produce freely, or once false, but at that time the world existed, so its past existence was necessary, as Agathon says.
claims: An eternal world would make its past existence always necessary, so not free.

rh-l2q2-d1e5018.summary: Further: if a man a was produced from eternity, he lived finitely (so time since is finite) or infinitely (so still alive). And if all men descend from a as from Adam, a was preceded by no one and lived a hundred years, so was not eternal.
claims: An eternal first man would imply finite time or immortality.

rh-l2q2-d1e5051.summary: Further: in any ordered succession, what is before none and after which all others come is simply first, so the whole multitude has a first and is finite. Hilary: what is from nothing has new being; Hugh: God could not have a coeternal creature.
claims: A succession with a first member is finite.
According to Hilary and Hugh, what is from nothing has new being.

rh-l2q2-d1e5096.summary: Anselm: if something is from nothing through something, that through which it is must be prior. Against the first thesis, arguments that an eternal world is contradictory. First: an infinite cannot be traversed, but an eternal world would have traversed infinitely many dead men, each once future and now past.
claims: An eternal world would require traversing an actual infinite.

rh-l2q2-d1e5125.summary: Second: an infinite cannot be exceeded, but in an eternal world one infinite multitude would exceed another, as fingers exceed men and lunar revolutions solar ones.
claims: Unequal infinities would be required.

rh-l2q2-d1e5141.summary: Third: God could have created and conserved a soul each day, so there would now be an actual infinite multitude; indeed with an eternal world there would be infinitely many immortal souls.
claims: An eternal world implies an actual infinity of souls.

rh-l2q2-d1e5157.summary: Fourth: each man was posterior to the sun, so the sun preceded the whole multitude, and in that prior no man existed, so no man was eternal.
claims: The sun's priority to each man implies priority to all.

rh-l2q2-d1e5168.summary: Fifth: the part would not be less than the whole, since removing ten from an infinite multitude leaves an infinite not less than the whole.
claims: Infinite multitudes violate part-whole axiom.

rh-l2q2-d1e5184.summary: Further: then God could not create more souls than he did, since there would be more than infinitely many.
claims: Infinite souls would limit divine power.

rh-l2q2-d1e5192.summary: Reply to the first: infinity is of continuous quantity or of multitude, actual or potential, as proportional parts in a continuum. 'Traversed' means for successive things being first future then past, for permanent things being moved across from end to end. 'An infinite cannot be traversed' is denied of an infinite quantity, since there is none.
claims: There is no actually infinite quantity to traverse.

rh-l2q2-d1e5241.summary: There is nothing absurd in granting that in an eternal world an infinite multitude was traversed, since in any time or any magnitude, however small, an infinite multitude is traversed, every magnitude being an infinite multitude of parts taken with copulated extreme. 'Each of them was future', pointing to all past men, is false as implying a falsehood, and 'the whole multitude was future' is to be denied, since an infinite multitude is not one multitude.
claims: Any finite magnitude contains an infinite multitude traversed.
An infinite multitude is not one whole multitude.

rh-l2q2-d1e5283.summary: Or: the whole multitude of past men was not future and so is not properly traversed. Those who deny 'a will be, so a is future' must deny 'the multitude is traversed', since 'multitude' supposits for a present multitude. 'Each was future, so the multitude was future' fails, like 'each choir of angels is past, so the multitude is past'. 'Infinitely many men were future' is true, and 'an infinite multitude is traversed' is true with 'infinite' taken syncategorematically.
claims: Distributive truths about each member do not transfer to the collective.
'Infinite' taken syncategorematically makes traversal claims true.

rh-l2q2-d1e5333.summary: Objection: each unit is traversed, so all units are, so the whole multitude is.
claims: From each traversed unit, all are traversed.

rh-l2q2-d1e5349.summary: Objection: the whole multitude was and no unit is, so the whole is past.
claims: The whole multitude is past.

rh-l2q2-d1e5356.summary: Objection: each unit is past, so all units are past.
claims: All units are past.

rh-l2q2-d1e5362.summary: Reply to the first: the inference fails, like 'each of these is distant from b, so all are distant from b' for all points of a line except its endpoint b. Since an infinity cannot be pointed out by a demonstrative, let a be a term for each such point: 'each a is distant from b' is true, 'all a's (collectively) are distant from b' false, since then something would lie between all a's and b.
claims: Distributive distance does not imply collective distance.

rh-l2q2-d1e5406.summary: Likewise denies 'each unit is past, so all units are past' taken collectively, though those who deny that 'fuit' expounds as 'est praeteritum' must deny the antecedent too.
claims: Collective 'all are past' does not follow from distributive.

rh-l2q2-d1e5422.summary: Objection: 'all units of this multitude are traversed', if false, is false wholly, so every man who was still is, or partly, so some who died are not traversed.
claims: The universal must be wholly or partly false.

rh-l2q2-d1e5440.summary: Reply: distinguish 'all' taken collectively or divisively. Divisively it is partly true and partly false, a universal all of whose singulars are true but one.
claims: Universals can have all true singulars but one.

rh-l2q2-d1e5453.summary: Likewise 'all parts of Socrates are less than Socrates' as a universal has every singular true except the one where all the parts together are taken, which converts with the collective sense, as 'all the apostles are twelve'. So 'all these units are traversed' as universal has one false singular, implying that infinitely many are some things once future and now past. Taken collectively it is a singular proposition, true or false only as a whole, and here false.
claims: A universal can have a false singular that converts with its collective sense.
Collective 'all' yields a singular proposition.

rh-l2q2-d1e5515.summary: Reply to the second: denies 'the whole multitude was and no unit is, so the whole is traversed', and the antecedent is false through its false implication that it is one whole multitude.
claims: An infinite multitude is not one whole.

rh-l2q2-d1e5527.summary: Reply to the third: grants the antecedent, denies the inference, though 'infinitely many men were future and past who are not now present' seems true, unless the relative 'who' carries a false implication.
claims: 'Infinitely many men were future and past' is true.

rh-l2q2-d1e5538.summary: Reply to the second principal objection: denies that an infinite cannot be exceeded; an infinite body would exceed an infinite surface and that an infinite line. But 'this infinite exceeds that, so doubly or triply' fails unless both are of the same kind of quantity.
claims: One infinite can exceed another of a different kind.

rh-l2q2-d1e5562.summary: To the proof: denies that there would be more lunar than solar revolutions, since though a thousand men have more fingers than men, infinitely many men do not; there are infinitely many of each.
claims: Infinite collections do not differ in number as finite ones do.

rh-l2q2-d1e5578.summary: Others answer that one infinite multitude is greater than another and grant more lunar than solar revolutions, holding that infinite ternaries and binaries stand in sesquialteral ratio and that addition can be made to an infinite. This is Grosseteste's view on the Physics.
claims: According to Grosseteste, infinite multitudes can be unequal.

rh-l2q2-d1e5598.summary: Reply to the third: the argument would not move Pythagoreans who held transmigration (Ovid, Metamorphoses XV). The immortality of the soul and the multiplication of souls with bodies is determined by faith alone. Or one may grant an actual infinite, denying that 'actual' means a true thing in this world, since in every continuum there are infinitely many actually distinct parts at distinct places (odd and even proportional parts a and b interleaved), which Aristotle calls potential because they are parts. For Aristotle there could be no actual infinite multitude, and he does not clearly hold transmigration.
claims: The soul's immortality is known by faith alone.
Every continuum contains infinitely many actually distinct parts.
Aristotle calls such parts potential because they are parts.

rh-l2q2-d1e5687.summary: Reply to the fourth: grants each man was posterior to the sun but denies that the whole multitude, or men collectively, was.
claims: Distributive posteriority does not imply collective posteriority.

rh-l2q2-d1e5699.summary: Reply to the fifth: grants a part can equal the whole, as the body equals the composite in extension, or matter and form in fire. With a quantity finite on one side and infinite on the other, the part is not less on the infinite side: a line infinite westward minus one foot at its eastern end is still infinite and not less. So for a multitude infinite in the past and finite now, removing ten leaves a multitude not less. Likewise a composite of the Word and humanity would be no greater than the Word, than which nothing greater can be thought. Every whole is greater than some part, not every part.
claims: A part can be equal to the whole in infinite quantities.
Not every whole is greater than each of its parts.

rh-l2q2-d1e5774.summary: Reply to the sixth: grants that, with infinitely many souls, God could literally not create more things than he created, yet he could create other souls, which would not be more things than a continuum with infinitely many proportional parts.
claims: With actual infinite souls God could create other but not more souls.

rh-l2q2-Dd1e5795.summary: Holcot holds that God can always make a better world, of the same species by enlargement or of a higher species, but cannot make the best he can. He answers Aristotle's arguments for one world through creation ex nihilo and distinct centers. God can do whatever does not make contradictories true together, and Anselm means only that nothing constrains God. Against Ockham, a man unable to sin need not differ in species, since impeccability comes by grace, and he argues that Ockham misreads Lombard and Lombard misreads Augustine.
claims: God can always make a better world.
God can do whatever does not make contradictories true together.
Impeccability comes by grace, not by a different species.

rh-l2q2-d1e5803.summary: Sixth article: whether God could make a better world than he made.

rh-l2q2-d1e5808.summary: Supposing by faith that God has intensively infinite power, produces freely, and the world is finitely good, three conclusions: God can make another world better than this and of the same species, differing only numerically; he can make a better one of another species; and he cannot make the best he can make, so God alone cannot make the best he can.
claims: God can make a better world of the same or another species.
God cannot make the best he can make.

rh-l2q2-d1e5837.summary: Proof of the first: God can do whatever involves no contradiction, and 'two suns', 'two moons', 'two worlds' involve none, so he could create other heavenly bodies of the same species differing only numerically.
claims: Two worlds of the same species involve no contradiction.

rh-l2q2-d1e5867.summary: Second: God can make a world infinitely better than this, though each is finite and of the same species, by enlarging spheres, stars, and elements proportionally without limit, since extension does not change species in homogeneous wholes (a sun twice as wide is still a sun). Likewise infinitely worse by diminishing parts.
claims: God can enlarge the world indefinitely without changing its species.
Size does not change species in homogeneous wholes.

rh-l2q2-d1e5922.summary: God can make a better world of another species, since above any species he can create a more perfect one, such as a sun of a higher species with more perfect operations, as man imagines better than an ox. But not a worse world of another species, since it would lack some species this world has and so not be a world.
claims: God can always create a more perfect species.
A world of a lower species would lack something essential to a world.

rh-l2q2-d1e5959.summary: Third: God cannot make the best he can, since for any good he can make a better; nor can he make as much or as quickly as he can.
claims: There is no best that God can make.

rh-l2q2-d1e5970.summary: Doubts from Aristotle's arguments in De caelo I for the unity of the world: the world consists of all its matter, so cannot be multiplied; heavy bodies would have no reason to move to this world's center rather than another's; and what naturally recedes from a place violently approaches it, so a heavy body anywhere would violently approach this world's center.
claims: According to Aristotle, the world is unique because it contains all matter and has a unique center.

rh-l2q2-d1e6009.summary: Second doubt, against the common supposition that God cannot do what involves contradiction: Anselm (Cur Deus homo II.17) says all necessity and impossibility are subject to God's will, which is subject to none; so if God could will man to be an ass it would be possible, and God does not necessarily not will it, so God can do the impossible.
claims: According to Anselm, necessity and impossibility are subject to God's will.

rh-l2q2-d1e6056.summary: Further: I can make something whose making involves contradiction, a copulative of contradictories, so God can.
claims: Making a contradictory copulative is making what involves contradiction.

rh-l2q2-d1e6070.summary: Third doubt: Lombard (II d. 44) and Augustine say God could have made man unable and unwilling to sin. Would such a man be of the same species as others? It seems not, since what belongs to one individual is not repugnant to another of the same species, and Christ's human nature, if the union were set aside, could sin.
claims: An impeccable man seems to differ in species from peccable men.

rh-l2q2-d1e6105.summary: Fourth doubt: whether one creature exceeds another infinitely in perfection. If Gabriel exceeds a fly only finitely, say a hundredfold, a hundred flies would equal Gabriel in perfection and their destruction would be as bad as the angel's.
claims: Finite ratios of perfection would let many lower creatures equal an angel.

rh-l2q2-d1e6136.summary: Further: if Gabriel exceeds a foot of fire by finite ratio a, God could create enough fire to equal Gabriel's perfection.
claims: Enough fire would equal an angel's perfection.

rh-l2q2-d1e6152.summary: Reply to the first doubt: Aristotle's arguments can be answered given the truth of faith.

rh-l2q2-d1e6165.summary: To the first: the inference fails, since the world can be multiplied by an agent that presupposes no matter but creates the whole. Though no matter is now in potency to the sun's form, another sun can be made, though no created agent presupposing matter can produce it.
claims: Creation without presupposed matter allows multiple worlds.

rh-l2q2-d1e6187.summary: To the second: a heavy body in each world would move naturally to the center of its own world.
claims: Each world would have its own natural center.

rh-l2q2-d1e6197.summary: To the third: denies that what naturally recedes from a place violently approaches it. Iron at the world's center naturally moves toward a magnet above it, and to avoid a vacuum; and fire at opposite points of the earth's surface naturally rises toward opposite points of the heavens, receding from one and approaching the other. So the same heavy body can naturally move toward different places in different worlds.
claims: The same body can naturally approach and recede from the same place in different situations.

rh-l2q2-d1e6252.summary: Reply to the second doubt: 'God can do whatever does not involve contradiction' is true rightly understood: God cannot do what, if done, would make contradictories true together, and can do everything else. Anselm means only that no coercion or prohibition constrains God's will and he lacks no power.
