God cannot will man to be an ass, and wills necessarily, not freely, that man not be an ass; he wills nothing necessarily to be except himself, but wills necessarily that things be as necessary complexes signify.
claims: God can do whatever does not make contradictories true together.
Anselm means only that nothing constrains God's will.
God necessarily wills that necessary truths hold.

rh-l2q2-d1e6321.summary: To the other: grants that a man can make what involves contradiction to make, a copulative of contradictories, but cannot make anything whose being made would make contradictories true together.
claims: One can make a contradictory proposition without making a contradiction true.

rh-l2q2-d1e6337.summary: Reply to the third doubt, Ockham's view: such a man would not be of our species. 'Man' can mean any composite of body and intellectual nature, which is not a most specific species, or one with a soul like ours, which is; one naturally impeccable is not of the same species as one naturally peccable, by the principle cited.
claims: According to Ockham, a naturally impeccable man would differ in species.

rh-l2q2-d1e6372.summary: Against: Lombard and Augustine speak of man already made, whom God could have made unable to sin, and God could not make him of another species, so Ockham's answer misses the point.
claims: Lombard and Augustine speak of man as made, not another species.

rh-l2q2-d1e6390.summary: Second: 'he cannot sin, so is of another species' fails, speaking of proximate power, as an impeded heavy body is not of another species than a falling one; Christ cannot sin yet is of our species. If God gave no precept, or refused to co-act with evil and prevented omissions, a man could not sin with proximate power, except as cold can heat by becoming hot, as a blind man can see or a cobbler consecrate bishops.
claims: Lacking proximate power to sin does not change species.

rh-l2q2-d1e6435.summary: Third: it is unfitting to say God could make an impeccable man because he could make a creature of another species, since what is not a rational mortal animal is not a man; he would make a creature called man, not a man.
claims: A creature of another species would not be a man.

rh-l2q2-d1e6455.summary: Confirmation: 'man' names a most specific species, not a genus, except by new imposition.
claims: 'Man' is a name of a most specific species.

rh-l2q2-d1e6464.summary: Fourth: such a creature is either free or not. If not, it is not rational; if free, given a precept it could freely obey or transgress.
claims: A free creature given a precept can transgress.

rh-l2q2-d1e6473.summary: Confirmation from Jerome (via Lombard II d. 25): God alone cannot sin; others, having free choice, can turn either way.
claims: According to Jerome, God alone is naturally impeccable.

rh-l2q2-d1e6486.summary: Fifth: such a creature could merit or not. If not, it would be damned without sin; if by nature, Pelagianism; if by grace, grace would be unnecessary, since it would be no more able to sin than a stone, and could not properly 'avoid' sin.
claims: A naturally impeccable creature would face dilemmas about merit.

rh-l2q2-d1e6508.summary: So Ockham neither follows Augustine nor does his argument conclude. Augustine means not that God could make a man naturally impeccable, but one endowed with gifts of grace and virtues such that God co-acts only to good, so that he could never sin with proximate power, like an impeded heavy body. Augustine there argues only that a nature unwilling to sin is better, against those who blame God for permitting temptation, and does not ask whether God could make man wholly unable to sin. So neither Ockham grasps Lombard's intention nor Lombard Augustine's; Lombard means impeccability by gifts, as in Christ's human nature and the blessed.
claims: Impeccability comes by gifts of grace, not nature.
Ockham misreads Lombard, and Lombard misreads Augustine.

rh-l2q2-d1e6580.summary: Reply to Ockham's principle: what belongs to one individual can be repugnant to another of the same species, as an intense heat excludes cold while a remiss one does not, a great fire acts at a mile while small ones do not, and a two-foot log is composed of two one-foot lengths while a one-foot log is not.
claims: Individuals of one species can differ in what is repugnant to them.

rh-l2q2-d1e6606.summary: The fourth doubt will be treated elsewhere.

rh-l2q2-Dd1e6613.summary: Against Aristotle's apparent view, Holcot holds with the theologians that future contingents are determinately true or false. A true future contingent can be such that it never was true, and contradictories cannot be true successively. Some such truths cannot change truth value, though human choices determine them, and God cannot begin to know anything.
claims: Future contingents are determinately true or false.
A true future contingent could never have been true.
God cannot begin to know anything.

rh-l2q2-d1e6621.summary: Seventh article: whether among future contingent propositions there is determinate truth in one contradictory and falsity in the other.

rh-l2q2-d1e6630.summary: Aristotle seems to say no, neither being true or false. The theologians hold the contrary: God knows the resurrection will be, and one side of every contradiction, else prophecy would be impossible. Either things are as 'a will be' signifies, so it is true, or not, so false.
claims: Theologians hold that future contingents have determinate truth.
Prophecy requires determinate truth about the future.

rh-l2q2-d1e6659.summary: Holcot's view with the common opinion: a future-tensed proposition is necessarily true or false, but true in such a way that it could never have been true, unlike past or present propositions not requiring a future truth, which once true are necessarily afterward 'were true'. In future contingents either contradictory can be true, but neither simultaneously nor successively.
claims: Future contingents are determinately true or false.
A true future contingent could never have been true.
Contradictory future contingents cannot be true successively.

rh-l2q2-d1e6684.summary: Corollaries: some proposition is true and can be false yet cannot cease to be true or begin to be false; some true from eternity could have been false from eternity, and if false now was false from eternity; Socrates can make a proposition to have been true from eternity that God never knew, yet God cannot begin to know it. Examples: 'Socrates will be blessed' and its contradictory.
claims: Some truths can be false yet cannot change truth value.
Human choice can determine what was eternally true.
God cannot begin to know anything.

rh-l2q2-d1e6726.summary: But some contingent propositions can cease to be true and begin to be false if they remain, like 'the Antichrist's soul will be created', 'judgment day will be', 'Socrates will be born at a', false after their events. Others concerning eternal beatitude or damnation, like 'Christ's soul will be blessed', 'Judas's soul will be damned', were true from eternity and can be false but cannot cease to be true.
claims: Some future propositions become false after their events.
Propositions about eternal states cannot change truth value.

rh-l2q2-d1e6770.summary: Some future propositions true only until a time, like 'Socrates will sin tomorrow', could never have been true before that time but cannot before then be true and false successively.
claims: Some future truths cannot change truth value before their time.

rh-l2q2-d1e6786.summary: So a future proposition is true because things will be as it denotes, though they could be otherwise, and it need not be that if it was true it will afterward be true to say it was true; in this it differs from past and present propositions.
claims: Future propositions are true by correspondence with what will be.
Past truth of future propositions is not necessary.

rh-l2q2-Dd1e6803.summary: Holcot affirms that God knows future contingents and asks whether he can reveal them so that they remain contingent. He professes to believe this even against arguments he cannot solve. He distinguishes senses of 'know' (God knows futures evidently but not as necessary), of 'certain', and of 'reveal'. He holds that God can knowingly assert a falsehood and deceive the deserving, but cannot lie, lacking disordered intent. God's knowledge is equivalent to whichever contradictory is true. All created knowledge of mutable objects, even in the blessed and Christ's soul, could become error without loss of essential beatitude.
claims: Revealed future contingents remain contingent.
God can assert falsehood and deceive but cannot lie.
All created knowledge of mutable things can become error.

rh-l2q2-d1e6808.summary: Eighth article: whether God can reveal future contingents. This presupposes that God knows future contingents, which must be granted (Lombard I d. 38-39).
claims: God knows future contingents.

rh-l2q2-d1e6819.summary: It is doubtful whether God can know more than he knows; Holcot has argued elsewhere against Ockham on this. The question is whether God can reveal future contingents and whether they remain contingent after revelation. Four parts: authorities, definitions, suppositions, and replies.
claims: Whether revealed futures remain contingent is the key question.

rh-l2q2-d1e6853.summary: Authorities: we must speak of God with fear and reverence (Augustine: philosophers speak freely, but we must keep to a fixed rule). So Holcot speaks without pertinacity, for inquiry. Even with no reason to reconcile foreknowledge and revelation with contingency, he would believe both, and count the best contrary arguments sophistical though no one could solve them. Anselm: a reason that scripture contradicts, however invincible, rests on no truth. Augustine: we embrace both foreknowledge and free will. Anselm: God can do what human reason cannot comprehend.
claims: Arguments against faith must be believed sophistical even if unsolved.
Foreknowledge, revelation, and contingency are believed compatible.

rh-l2q2-d1e6936.summary: Definitions. 'Know' is said broadly of any cognition of true or false, complex or incomplex; strictly of evident assent to a truth without fear ('the wall is white', 'the sun will rise tomorrow'); most strictly of evident assent to a truth that cannot be otherwise (Aristotle: knowledge through causes; Anselm: what can not be cannot be known by certain reason). God knows everything in the first sense, future contingents in the second, but not in the third, since they could never have been true. In the second sense the same assent can become error when the thing changes, since 'knowledge' connotes that things are as the assent says; so one can err through knowledge, though not 'by' knowledge.
claims: God knows future contingents with evident assent but not as necessary.
The same assent can be knowledge or error as things change.
'Knowledge' is a connotative term.

rh-l2q2-d1e7046.summary: Second: 'certain' is said either because one believes as things in fact are, or because things are so and cannot be otherwise. In the first sense God certifies the blessed that they will always be blessed, though their certainty could have been error by absolute power. In the second he cannot, since that would contradict his omnipotence to annihilate the creature (Anselm).
claims: God certifies the blessed in the sense of true belief, not necessity.
The certainty of the blessed could be error by absolute power.

rh-l2q2-d1e7094.summary: Third: 'reveal' means either causing a new assent to a true complex in another's intellect (with fear, opinion; without, knowledge), or simply causing a new assent to a complex. In the first sense 'God revealed to Socrates that judgment day will be' is contingent, 'revelation' being connotative of truth. In the second it is necessary and independent of the future, and God can reveal a falsehood if he wills to deceive, which is not unfitting, since truth itself may cause falsity.
claims: 'Revelation' in one sense connotes truth and is contingent.
In another sense God can reveal falsehoods.

rh-l2q2-d1e7182.summary: Exposition of 'Christ asserted', 'God promised', 'Christ swore': to assert is to utter a proposition wishing the hearer to believe it true, not requiring one believe it. Holcot sees no contradiction in God knowingly asserting a falsehood, though God cannot lie, since a lie is a false signification with disordered intent to deceive (Augustine), and God has no disordered intent. God can assert falsehood with intent to deceive, since creatures can deserve deception, as the demons do. Augustine says God deceives through bad angels and men, commanded Israel to despoil Egypt, and sent a lying spirit to Ahab; Christ's virgin birth deceived the devil; Rebecca and Jacob deceived Isaac by the Spirit's counsel; Judith deceived Holofernes; God told Joshua to lay an ambush. So God can say falsehoods or promise and not perform.
claims: God can knowingly assert falsehood but cannot lie.
Lying requires a disordered intention to deceive.
God can deceive those who deserve it.

rh-l2q2-d1e7301.summary: Fifth: God is the true knowledge of every truth, whether expressed by future, past, or present propositions, yet he knows the future such that he could never have known it, and can be knowledge equivalent to two contradictories successively, with or without change in things.
claims: God's knowledge is equivalent to whichever contradictory is true.

rh-l2q2-d1e7321.summary: Sixth: every created knowledge is limited to signifying as it denotes, so can become error if its object is mutable. The many created cognitions in the blessed and in Christ's soul, about the sun's motion or eclipses, could become errors if God willed, so 'a blessed one is deceived' and 'God deceives' could be true, and by communication of idioms 'God is deceived'. Only God cannot err; no creature's knowledge is immune, and the blessed would be no less blessed if deceived about creatures, since such certainty contributes nothing to essential beatitude.
claims: Every created knowledge of a mutable object can become error.
Only God cannot err.
Certainty about creatures is not part of essential beatitude.

rh-l2q2-Dd1e7373.summary: Holcot uses rules from the art of obligations (positio, depositio, impossibility per accidens) to answer the principal arguments on future contingents and revelation. He grants that revealed futures, scripture's predictions included, remain contingent, and that one can merit by false faith. 'Christ asserted this' is contingent when it depends on a future truth. Christ's created knowledge could err but his increate knowledge cannot. Willing someone to believe a falsehood is not willing to deceive. By communication of idioms 'God can be deceived'. Present choices can make past persons prophets or not, since 'prophet' is connotative. Prophecy has only conditional necessity of the consequence (Anselm, Boethius). God fulfills promises as surely as if he could not fail.
claims: Revealed futures, including scripture's, remain contingent.
One can merit by false faith.
Prophecy has necessity of the consequence, not of the consequent.
Present choices can determine whether someone was a prophet.

rh-l2q2-d1e7378.summary: Ninth article: first some logical rules from the art of obligations are supposed.

rh-l2q2-d1e7387.summary: First: when the opponent posits a case and the respondent admits it, the respondent must answer according to the case; 'let it be so' or equivalent creates a positio, a species of obligation.
claims: Admitting a posited case obliges answering according to it.

rh-l2q2-d1e7405.summary: Second: whatever follows formally from what is posited and granted must be granted, whatever is repugnant denied; irrelevant propositions are answered according to their own quality.
claims: Consequences of the positum must be granted, repugnants denied.

rh-l2q2-d1e7416.summary: Third: every positio is equivalent to a depositio of the contradictory, since the respondent's answers are the same either way.
claims: Positing one contradictory is deposing the other.

rh-l2q2-d1e7439.summary: Fourth: given a false contingent positum, it is not unfitting to grant something impossible per accidens.
claims: Under a false positum one may grant impossibilities per accidens.

rh-l2q2-d1e7448.summary: Replies to the seventh and eighth principal arguments. If God knew 'a will be' and it was written on a wall, 'what was written was true' is now necessary as a proposition, yet true such that it could never have been true. 'a will be' and 'a can not happen' stand together. 'Let it be posited that a will not happen' creates a new positio deposing 'a will be', so 'God knew a would be' must be denied; 'yesterday you granted the opposite without obligation' is irrelevant and true, and 'you responded badly yesterday' follows and may be granted as impossible per accidens under the positum.
claims: Future contingents can be known yet possibly fail.
Positing their failure deposes the earlier truth, yielding impossibilities per accidens.

rh-l2q2-d1e7539.summary: To the third: the assumption is false; there are two propositions that can be true yet neither together nor successively. Something can be true and possibly not, yet not become true, as 'Socrates is predestined': if it could begin to be true at a, then before a 'Socrates is not predestined' was true from eternity and God knew 'he is not predestined and will be', so he would not have eternal life.
claims: Some truths can neither begin nor cease to be true.
Predestination cannot begin.

rh-l2q2-d1e7585.summary: To the fourth: denies 'b can be true after a was true'; grants 'after a was true, b can be true', which means a is true now and b can be true later, not that 'b is true' can be true after a. Or distinguish composite and divided sense.
claims: Scope distinctions dissolve successive-truth arguments.

rh-l2q2-d1e7614.summary: To the fifth: denies the inference, since the antecedent has a cause of truth and the consequent none, signifying that a is not future though it could always have been.
claims: Beginning to be future is impossible.

rh-l2q2-d1e7628.summary: To the sixth: for Aristotle, 'the sun moves' or 'Socrates is white' depend on no future contingent ad utrumlibet, since when the sun moves, 'it will move' is not contingent; not every future proposition is in contingent matter. Nor does 'Socrates is, so Socrates will be' hold, granting there may be a last instant of Socrates' being.
claims: Not every future proposition is contingent.
'Socrates is' does not imply 'Socrates will be'.

rh-l2q2-d1e7696.summary: Reply to the eighth principal argument: grants that God could reveal future contingents so that they remain contingent after revelation, so whatever scripture reveals about judgment day and the resurrection could be false, and grants that 'Abraham merited in false faith' is possible. One merits by false faith as by true, since merit comes not from the truth of what is believed, which is not in one's power, but from God commanding belief and accepting the act.
claims: Revealed futures remain contingent.
Scripture's predictions could be false.
One can merit by false faith as by true.

rh-l2q2-d1e7731.summary: Objection: then Christ's soul could have been deceived and 'Christ preached a falsehood' possible. Reply: 'Christ preached this' is contingent, since it converts with 'Christ foreknew this and it was true'; so after 'you will deny me three times', 'Christ asserted this to Peter' was contingent, and likewise 'Christ's soul believes judgment day will be'. All these difficulties would be solved if the argument about Peter's denial were solved.
claims: 'Christ preached this' is contingent when it depends on a future truth.

rh-l2q2-d1e7790.summary: Some say that after Christ asserted it to Peter he could never have asserted it, but must grant 'Christ preached falsehood' as impossible per accidens under a false positum. This answer does not satisfy Holcot.
claims: The impossible per accidens answer is insufficient.

rh-l2q2-d1e7810.summary: Against it: let a be Christ's vocal assertion of judgment day at time b; 'this was uttered by Christ at b' is necessary per accidens and 'this was false at b' contingent, so 'a falsehood was uttered by Christ at b' is contingent.
claims: Christ's past utterance plus possible falsity makes his uttering falsehood contingent.

rh-l2q2-d1e7832.summary: Further: Christ's soul asserted a, which may be false, so 'Christ's soul asserted a falsehood' and 'was deceived' are contingent. This differs from 'a was known by God at b', whose major is itself contingent.
claims: Christ's soul could have been deceived.

rh-l2q2-d1e7854.summary: 'Christ's soul asserted a when it uttered a at b' is simply necessary if true, so now necessary, depending on no future more than 'Peter asserted'. But 'Christ's soul was deceived', 'believed falsehood' are contingent, while 'Christ's soul was blessed' is now impossible to deny. Christ's human nature did not lie, since it uttered nothing with disordered intent to deceive.
claims: Christ's past assertion is necessary, but its truth is contingent.
Christ's human nature did not lie.

rh-l2q2-d1e7895.summary: Objection: Christ willed his disciples to believe what he uttered, which may be false, so he willed them to believe falsehood, so to deceive them.
claims: Christ would have willed his disciples to believe a falsehood.

rh-l2q2-d1e7911.summary: Grants it is contingent, but it will never be true that Christ willed his disciples to believe falsehoods; otherwise God's power would be too restricted if he could not now make judgment day not occur or annihilate an angel. Likewise between 'you will deny me' and the denial, 'Peter will deny Christ' was contingent, so Christ could have asserted falsehood, and it was in Peter's power, or anyone's who could have killed him, that Christ asserted falsehood, but not that Christ lied.
claims: Peter could have made Christ's prediction false but not made Christ a liar.
God's power to falsify revealed futures must be preserved.

rh-l2q2-d1e7953.summary: Objection: Christ knew he asserted a falsehood with intent to make Peter believe it, so there was false signification with intent to deceive, which was contingent in the interval.
claims: Christ would have spoken falsely with intent to deceive.

rh-l2q2-d1e7990.summary: Reply: Christ has two knowledges, increate and created, and two intentions, the divine will and a created volition. Created knowledge can become error when its object changes, since knowledge of 'a will be' stays such; increate knowledge cannot err, being knowledge of 'a will be' yet able to be of 'a will not be' without change, by its unlimitedness. By increate intention Christ could make Peter believe falsehood; by created intention 'Christ intended to deceive Peter' was impossible. Willing someone to believe a falsehood is not willing to deceive, as when I sincerely assert the king is not sitting; properly, willing to deceive is willing someone to believe something while believing it is not so. 'Christ's soul was deceived' was contingent, so by communication of idioms 'God can be deceived', as 'God can die'.
claims: Christ's created knowledge could err; his increate knowledge cannot.
Willing someone to believe a falsehood is not willing to deceive.
By communication of idioms, 'God can be deceived' is true.

rh-l2q2-d1e8103.summary: Further: it seems 'God asserted a falsehood known to be false with intent to deceive' must be granted as possible, if asserting is just speaking with intent that the hearer believe; and it would not be unfitting if God wrote 'judgment day will not be' in a book intending some wicked man to believe it, or formed such sounds in the air. So after Christ's assertion these were possible: Christ willed to deceive Peter; Christ said a falsehood known as false; Christ was not deceived while his soul was. None is true, but each is possible by communication of idioms.
claims: God can possibly assert a known falsehood with intent to deceive.
Paradoxical claims about Christ are possible by communication of idioms though none is true.

rh-l2q2-d1e8157.summary: Reply to the second sub-argument: denies that one justly damned a hundred years ago could now never have been justly damned. It is possible the Sadducee believed a falsehood, but it does not follow that he could be unjustly damned, since, if 'the resurrection will not be' were true, he would have believed a truth he should not have believed and refused a falsehood he was commanded to believe.
claims: Damnation for disobeying a command to believe is just even if the content proves false.

rh-l2q2-d1e8191.summary: Reply to the third: admitting the case, Socrates never willed contrary to God in willing Plato's damnation, yet he willed the opposite of what he was commanded, so he sinned and was justly damned.
claims: Sin consists in violating the precept, not in diverging from God's good pleasure.

rh-l2q2-d1e8204.summary: Reply to the fourth: grants that it is now in my power to make someone dead a hundred years a prophet or not, since 'prophet' is a connotative term signifying one who foretells truly, and I can freely do or not do what he foretold. So until fulfillment 'he prophesied' is contingent: 'Job prophesied the resurrection' is contingent today, and someone could have spoken truly all his life and yet never have uttered a true proposition.
claims: 'Prophet' is connotative, so present choices determine whether past persons were prophets.
'Job prophesied the resurrection' is contingent today.

rh-l2q2-d1e8256.summary: On the definition of prophecy as announcing with immobile truth: this is the immobile truth of many contingents, as Anselm speaks of the immobile necessity of the future, saying what God proposes cannot not be future, and that a future thing is necessarily future.
claims: Prophecy's immobile truth is compatible with contingency.

rh-l2q2-d1e8285.summary: Anselm (De concordia) distinguishes preceding necessity, which causes a thing to be, and subsequent necessity, which the thing makes; so conditionals like 'if something is future it will be', 'if God knew it would be it will be', 'if Job prophesied the resurrection it will be' are necessary. Boethius distinguishes simple and conditional necessity; others necessity of the consequence and of the consequent. Prophecy has consequential, conditional necessity, not absolute. Anselm: a future sedition can fail to happen, yet a future thing necessarily is future. So something future can be non-future, though nothing is at once future and not, though these locutions are improper.
claims: Prophecy has necessity of the consequence, not of the consequent.
A future thing can fail to be future, though not simultaneously.

rh-l2q2-d1e8376.summary: Objection: what is not future but can be can begin to be future. Reply: the argument uses improper locutions, since nothing is such that it neither is nor will be yet can be future; properly it means 'a neither is nor will be and yet can be', and then 'a can begin to be future' follows. Reply to the fifth: 1 Corinthians 15 means 'if Christ has not the power to raise the dead, neither did he rise', proving the possibility and persuading the truth of the resurrection; the consequence is good though the antecedent impossible (Augustine). Micaiah's conditional is true, with contingent antecedent and consequent.
claims: Paul's argument concerns the power to raise the dead.
Micaiah's conditional has contingent parts.

rh-l2q2-d1e8432.summary: Reply to the sixth: grants 'Christ's soul was blessed' is contingent, 'blessed' expounded as 'enjoys and always will enjoy God'.
claims: 'Christ's soul was blessed' is contingent because 'blessed' includes the future.

rh-l2q2-d1e8444.summary: Reply to the seventh: how God can and cannot certify follows from the eighth article. 'Christ is truth and cannot deny himself' means God fulfills his promises as certainly as if he could not fail to; likewise 'all must be fulfilled' means they will be fulfilled as if they could not be impeded. Reply to the eighth: angels are confirmed, though it can be that they never were. The rest is answered by the articles. The third question follows.
claims: God fulfills promises as surely as if he could not fail.
Angels are confirmed though they possibly never were.
